title: Asset inventory, threat modeling and risk
subtitle: Identify important assets, model plausible failure paths, estimate likelihood and impact, and assign risk treatments.
description: Identify important assets, model plausible failure paths, estimate likelihood and impact, and assign risk treatments. Guided explanations, six original visual diagrams, safe practice, trusted resource links, worked examples and a randomized quiz.

blocks.text: Lesson 2 — Asset inventory, threat modeling and risk

LEARNING OUTCOME
Identify important assets, model plausible failure paths, estimate likelihood and impact, and assign risk treatments.

Safety rule: work only with devices, accounts and training applications you own or have explicit written permission to assess. Use synthetic information. A public system or a suspicious person is not permission.

Record each service, data handled, business purpose, owner, exposure, dependencies and recovery needs. Classify data by sensitivity, not curiosity. Keep inventories in approved workspaces and remove unneeded copies. Unknown or ownerless assets are hard to protect because nobody can make a decision about them.

Visual 2/6 — Threat source. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: Ask what could go wrong, what assumptions must be true, what weak points exist, and what could prevent or detect the event. Structured models such as STRIDE can help brainstorm, but they do not prove a threat will occur. Include outages, misconfiguration, accidental deletion, supplier failures and mistakes as well as malicious events.

blocks.caption: Visual 3/6 — Weakness path. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 4/6 — Likelihood × impact. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: Estimate likelihood and impact using the organization’s agreed scale and document uncertainty. Risk can be mitigated, avoided, transferred in part, or consciously accepted by an accountable owner with a review date. A numeric score supports judgement; it does not replace judgement.

blocks.caption: Visual 5/6 — Risk register. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 6/6 — Treatment options. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: Practice checklist: (1) read the lab rules, (2) use fabricated data or an isolated training target, (3) predict what the control should do, (4) test one small condition, (5) save only minimal evidence, and (6) explain the defensive follow-up. Stop and ask the owner if any target or action is outside the approved scope.

blocks.output: An illustrative score only; organizations must define their own scale.

blocks.question: Why is an asset owner useful in a risk register?
options: They can make decisions and accept or treat risk
blocks.explanation: An owner is accountable for treatment decisions and review.
blocks.hint: Use the lesson definitions and authorization boundary to reason through the options.

blocks.question: Why should risk scores state their assumptions?
options: To make uncertainty visible and revisit it when facts change
To guarantee the number is exact
blocks.explanation: Scores depend on context and assumptions; document both.
blocks.hint: Use the lesson definitions and authorization boundary to reason through the options.

blocks.question: Which approach better protects private information?
options: Copy all customer records for convenience
Use synthetic data and collect only necessary, authorized evidence
blocks.explanation: Data minimization and redaction reduce privacy and exposure risks.
blocks.hint: Use the lesson definitions and authorization boundary to reason through the options.

blocks.question: What is a sound step after applying a fix?
options: Retest the same authorized condition and document the result
blocks.explanation: Retesting verifies the correction and preserves a useful record.
blocks.hint: Use the lesson definitions and authorization boundary to reason through the options.

blocks.question: What should happen when a target is outside scope?
options: Stop and ask the owner to clarify permission
blocks.explanation: Scope is a boundary; do not proceed without permission.
blocks.hint: Use the lesson definitions and authorization boundary to reason through the options.
